claims: The 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution was ratified on August 18, 1920.
The 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution prohibited denying citizens the right to vote based on sex.
The 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution effectively granted women nationwide suffrage.
Tennessee provided the final necessary vote for ratification of the 19th Amendment.
The 19th Amendment was formally certified on August 26, 1920, by Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby.
The 19th Amendment states that '[t]he right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of sex'.
The women's suffrage movement gained momentum during World War I.

Many women of color—particularly African Americans, Native Americans, and Asian Americans—remained disenfranchised by state-level voter suppression, such as poll taxes and literacy tests, until the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
Key advocates of the women's suffrage movement included Ida B. Wells, Alice Paul, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Lucretia Mott, and Susan B. Anthony.
The National American Woman Suffrage Association (NAWSA) played a key role in organizing the women's suffrage movement.
The 19th Amendment immediately enfranchised 26 million American women in time for the 1920 presidential election.
The 19th Amendment legally validated women's right to participate in local, state, and national elections.
